section: Situational variations your robot must learn for essentially every task

text: Retrieve a specific medical item (e.g., EpiPen, inhaler, ice pack, heating pad).
Install or seat a delicate component (e.g., seating an NVMe SSD or RAM stick until it clicks).
Dust computer internals using compressed air while holding fans stationary to prevent over-spinning.
Clean out and replace an aquarium or terrarium filter.
Check the temperature gradient of a reptile enclosure.
Sick-day care: take a temperature, bring fluids, tissues, and a heating pad, clean up after vomiting, fetch an inhaler or EpiPen, bring medication on the person's own schedule and log it.

Kids: bedtime routine (bath-water temperature check, pajamas, story, night light, checking on a sleeping child), bottle and formula prep, sterilizing, supervised play (catch, hide-and-seek, card and board games), reading aloud.

Accessibility beyond mobility: describe layout and obstacles for low-vision residents, read mail and labels aloud, flash lights for the doorbell and alarms for deaf residents, keep furniture in consistent positions, dementia-friendly routines (labels, door checks).

section: Emergency response (must-have). Detection and alerting are covered well, but active response is thin.
text: Respond: shut off the main water, a fixture valve, or gas; use a fire extinguisher; evacuate people and pets; call emergency services and relay the address and symptoms; unlock the door and guide responders; fetch the AED and first-aid kit; run a power-outage routine (flashlights, unplug sensitive electronics, protect the fridge and freezer); shelter during severe weather; know where the breaker panel and shutoffs are.
Take and relay messages ("tell the kids dinner's ready"), announce visitors, set up and tidy for video calls, take group photos.

section: Reaching, climbing, and fixing. Tool handling stops at basic hand tools, and there's no height access.
text: Use a step stool, ladder, or reacher (with stability checks) for high shelves, ceiling bulbs, attic hatches, and hanging lights.

text: Small plumbing and fixes: unclog sinks and shower drains, fix a running toilet, reset a garbage disposal, clear a printer jam, bleed a radiator.
Hazardous and bulky disposal: batteries, bulbs, e-waste, paint, aerosols, old medications, cooking oil, old furniture; stage items until drop-off day and transport them.

Charge or swap its own battery; wipe its cameras and sensors; get up after a fall; wait in an unobtrusive spot; quiet and privacy modes (cameras and mics off in bathrooms and bedrooms); knock before entering an occupied room; ask for remote help; log its own faults.

Away mode. Your departure routine covers daily exits. Add a vacation or house-sitting mode: arm the alarm, set lights on timers, bring in mail and packages, water plants, check for leaks and pests, run taps, check the freezer after an outage, care for pets, send status photos.

Vehicles, bikes, and errands (only if scope goes past the property line). Refuel, check and inflate tires, top off washer fluid, change wipers, jump-start, change a flat, scrape ice and snow, check the back seat before locking, check a car seat; lube a bike chain, patch a flat, charge an e-bike; curbside pickup, pharmacy, post office, donation and return drop-offs.

Situational variations. Apartments and condos (elevators, shared laundry, HOA rules), regional standards (metric vs. imperial, front vs. top-load, induction vs. gas, shoes-off homes), languages, accents, and speech differences, residents with disabilities or dementia, residents' emotional states, and robot-side degradation (dirty camera, low battery, network down, a failing arm).
“Fix this up.” The robot must determine what looks wrong before deciding what actions to take.
“Make this usable again.” Could mean clearing clutter, reconnecting something, cleaning it, reorganizing it, or finding missing components.
“Check the house before we leave.” It has to inspect locks, windows, appliances, pets, lights, faucets, garage doors, and other household-specific concerns.
“Get the house ready for bed.” It must combine locking doors, dimming lights, closing blinds, checking appliances, preparing rooms, and possibly pet routines.
“Don’t disturb my setup.” It has to understand which relationships between objects must remain unchanged.
“Clean the spots people usually miss.” Requires knowledge of common cleaning failures.
“Find where that smell is coming from.” Requires active investigation across rooms and possible causes.
“The room feels weird. Check it.” Very ambiguous: temperature, smell, noise, lighting, objects out of place, or equipment malfunction.
“Make sure nothing looks wrong.” General anomaly detection across an open world.
“Set things up how I like them.” Requires user-specific configuration memory.
“Roll this cable so it doesn’t get tangled.” Requires predicting future physical behavior.
“Baby-proof this room.” Requires predicting how a small child could interact with the environment.
“Take this apart without breaking anything.” Requires discovering hidden fasteners and assembly sequence.
“Do this before it becomes a problem.” Requires predictive maintenance reasoning.
“Reorganize this room now that we bought this new thing.” Requires adapting an existing organization system.
“ untangle these cords without unplugging the computer.” Requires topology reasoning while simultaneously identifying and protecting active power constraints.

“Optimize the house for low energy today.” Requires reasoning across multiple systems: lowering the thermostat, closing blinds facing the sun, turning off vampire-draw electronics, and delaying the dishwasher until off-peak hours.
“Take a good family photo.” Requires aesthetic judgment regarding lighting, framing, composition, and timing (waiting for everyone to look and smile).
“Turn off the smoke alarm, it’s annoying.” Requires telling a nuisance from a safety function before complying, verifying, or refusing.
“Something’s burning!” Requires locating the source, then choosing between cutting power or gas, smothering, evacuating, or calling for help in seconds.
“The power just went out.” Requires working out what matters right now: light, fridge, medical devices, kids, phones.
“Tell me when the laundry’s done.” Requires monitoring cues (sound, status light) and choosing when and how to notify.
“Learn the house.” Requires mapping rooms, objects, owners, no-go zones, shutoff locations, and the emergency plan, including in a home that isn’t yours.
“We’re on a call, be quiet.” Requires switching to a quiet mode and blocking noisy interruptions (doorbell, vacuum, notifications).
“Make Grandma comfortable.” Requires adapting temperature, seating, lighting, and reach to one specific person.
“Calm the dog down.” Requires reading animal state (storm, fireworks, separation) and choosing a response.
